1.pericope_label: Son of man, set thy face toward the mountains of Israel, and prophesy against them
debates: Whether Israel here means the ten tribes or Judea
Why the address is made to mountains rather than men
outliers: Calvin holds against Gill, Clarke and Henry that the northern kingdom is meant, arguing that the Assyrian took only the flower of the people and left the commonalty behind, so that a population remained to be judged

Calvin and Gill both hear an insult in the address to the mountains, since a people who had so often put the word away were unworthy of it, Calvin recalling the prophet who turned from a king to speak to an altar
Henry observes that God sometimes ruins idolatries by the hands of idolaters, the Chaldeans being the greatest admirers of their own gods and the greatest despisers of everyone else
themes: A judge who fixes his eyes on the prisoner while sentencing him
Hills called to hear what men refuse to
High places rebuilt after one king pulled them down
An idol made into a desolation

3.pericope_label: And say, Ye mountains of Israel, hear the word of the Lord God; Thus saith the Lord God to the mountains, and to the hills, to the rivers, and to the valleys; Behold, I, even I, will bring a sword upon you
debates: What the word rendered rivers means
Whether the images are sun images or named from inflamed desire
Whether the mountains are still addressed by the closing verse
outliers: Calvin grants that the word for images derives from heat but calls the sun reading too contracted, preferring to name the idols from the mad love with which their worshippers were seized
Ellicott finds poetic justice in the corpses, since nothing was so defiling under the law as the touch of a dead body, so the idols are now defiled by the dead who worshipped them
Clarke reports the literal fulfilment from the account in Baruch, that the Chaldeans opened the sepulchres of the principal people and threw the bones about on every side
themes: A sword that cannot cut a mountain
Rites carried into a ravine for the shade
A command against Canaan turned back on Israel
Altars fouled by the bones of their own worshippers

8.pericope_label: Yet will I leave a remnant, that ye may have some that shall escape the sword among the nations, when ye shall be scattered through the countries
debates: What it means that God is broken
Why only a remnant is brought to repentance
Whether the promise is pardon or only survival
outliers: Ellicott takes the passive verb as a middle in a transitive sense, so that God has broken their whorish heart, while Wesley reads it as grief and Calvin offers two senses and prefers the one where God is worn down by their obstinacy
Calvin denies that simple pardon is offered, since the safety promised lies in exile itself, so that the life granted is a wretched one obtained through a kind of death
Ellicott reads the remnant as part of a plan pursued from the beginning and set out by Paul, looking far beyond this captivity, as the prophecy of Zechariah uttered after the return shows
themes: Mercy rejoicing against judgment
A prodigal who remembers home only when starving
Space to repent without the grace to do it
Eyes that chose the gods and then adored them

10.pericope_label: Thus saith the Lord God; Smite with thine hand, and stamp with thy foot, and say, Alas for all the evil abominations of the house of Israel! for they shall fall by the sword, by the famine, and by the pestilence
debates: Why the prophet is given a gesture as well as words
Whether the gestures license anything in public worship
Whether each punishment is assigned to a particular class
outliers: Henry defends the gestures against those who call them antic and ridiculous, holding that a man who knows the worth of souls will be laughed at by the wits if he may edify the weak; Clarke attacks those who argue from the verse for clapping and stamping in worship, since consistency would require copying the prophet other typical actions too
Ellicott warns against over-reading the arrangement of the three punishments, since all of them fall on the whole people and those who escape one will fall by another
Calvin explains that the three are named not because God punishes only so, having innumerable hidden methods, but because this scourge is the most familiar
themes: A man contending with a prophet and not noticing who sent him
Arrows that reach further than the archers do
The saddest death kept for the most cautious man
Incense answered at last by the smell of the dead

13.pericope_label: So will I stretch out mine hand upon them, and make the land desolate, yea, more desolate than the wilderness toward Diblath, in all their habitations: and they shall know that I am the Lord
debates: Where the wilderness named at the close lay
Whether the text should read a different place name altogether
Whether the phrase is a comparison or a boundary
outliers: Clarke reports the conjecture that the place is really Riblah, where the princes of Israel were killed and Zedekiah blinded, the difference lying in two letters often scarcely distinguishable in manuscripts, and notes that copies collated by Kennicott read it that way while all the ancient versions do not
Calvin places the wilderness beyond Israel in Syria, thought by some to be Antioch, against Clarke, Ellicott and Wesley who all put it on the border of Moab

Calvin rejects the rendering that makes the phrase a boundary running from the desert to that place, taking the particle as comparison, and argues that the exiles had already crossed that desert so the contrast with fertile country would wake them
themes: A god ridiculed by the corpse of its own worshipper
Incense offered to please an adulterer
A hand stretched out because a nod would not be noticed
One lost letter worth the pains of recovering
